beads.title: Honour Retry-After on 429/503 from every /machine/ endpoint, not just register
beads.description: Control can ask this node to back off and this node only listens on one of the two requests it makes. At commit e2ed432399c9b0fda7aa14e9eb27784d2d893c55, capability version 147 (tailcfg/tailcfg.go:198, 2026-09-09) is "Client handles 429/503 responses with retry-after headers to /machine/ endpoints", added by 29cfb0b4c, and it has three separable parts. (1) WHICH RESPONSES COUNT: control/controlclient/direct.go:623 isRateLimitedResponse returns true for 429 always, and for 503 ONLY when a Retry-After header is present -- a bare 503 stays a generic failure subject to backoff. That asymmetry is the refusal to port, not decoration, and it is the easy thing to get wrong. Both the register path (direct.go:828, which previously tested res.StatusCode == 429 literally) and the map path now go through it. (2) WHERE IT IS CHECKED: sendMapRequest (direct.go:1196) turns a rate-limited non-200 MAP response into a typed rateLimitError instead of the generic "initial fetch failed %d: %.200s". (3) HOW LONG TO WAIT: auto.go:655 waitRetryAfter caps the server-requested delay at maxRetryWindow = 5 * time.Minute (auto.go:41), and in mapRoutine (auto.go:631) a rate-limited poll SKIPS bo.BackOff entirely rather than backing off as well; updateRoutine (auto.go:97) and authRoutine (auto.go:369) were folded onto the same helper. This repository has part of (1) and none of (2) or (3). ts_control/src/tokio/register.rs:261 tests status.as_u16() == 429 and nothing else, so a 503 with a Retry-After is an opaque HTTP error here. ts_control/src/tokio/map_stream.rs:543 collapses every non-success map status into MapStreamError::Http and reads no header at all, so ts_control::Error::RateLimited is constructed in exactly one place in the whole tree (register.rs:274) and the map poll can never produce one. The consequence is that the rate-limit arm that already exists at ts_control/src/tokio/client.rs:659 -- which correctly waits the server-requested cooldown INSTEAD of the local backoff -- is reachable only for the re-register inside the poll loop, which is exactly what its own log message at client.rs:671 says ("rate-limited the map-poll re-register"). A control plane that rate-limits the map poll itself gets a client that reconnects on its own backoff schedule and ignores the cooldown it was given. The work is small and lands in three named places. Add the 429-always/503-with-Retry-After predicate once and call it from both status checks; give map_stream.rs a rate-limit arm above its !status.is_success() arm that parses the header with the EXISTING parse_retry_after (register.rs:308) and returns RateLimited; and add the 5-minute cap at the wait site. Note on the two caps, because they are different bounds and both are upstream's: parse_retry_after already clamps at MAX_RETRY_AFTER = 1 hour, mirroring Go's parseRateLimitError, and upstream KEPT that -- maxRetryWindow is a second, tighter cap applied at the point of waiting, not a replacement. Port both. Test the refusals, which is where the divergences are: a 503 WITHOUT Retry-After must still take the generic backoff path and must not become a RateLimited; a rate-limited poll must not also advance the backoff counter; and a Retry-After longer than five minutes must wait five minutes, not an hour and not the raw value. See PORTING.md section A row 147.

beads.title: Stop one-cgnat?v=false from disabling the CGNAT collapse at every peer count
beads.description: The host route table this repository just taught itself to bound is still unbounded whenever control says one-cgnat?v=false. At commit e2ed432399c9b0fda7aa14e9eb27784d2d893c55, net/routemanager/routemanager.go models the decision as TailnetConfig.OneCGNAT, a plain bool, and RouteManager.cgnatThreshold() (routemanager.go:887) returns 1 when it is set and the cgnatThreshold constant (10_000, routemanager.go:148) otherwise. So the DISABLING attribute only declines the FORCED collapse; the ceiling still applies, and wantCoarse := len(rm.cgnatPfxs) > rm.cgnatThreshold() (routemanager.go:959) still installs the single 100.64.0.0/10 once more than 10000 distinct CGNAT peer routes exist. There is no value of the attribute that switches the ceiling off -- that is the point of modelling it as a threshold rather than as a boolean over the collapse. This repository ported the collapse in #438 and inverted that rule. The merged cgnat_threshold maps Some(false) to usize::MAX, commented "unreachable so the fold never fires", so with one-cgnat?v=false set the collapse can never happen at any peer count: a tailnet above the threshold programs one /32 per peer here where a Go client programs a single /10. The merged test host_routes_collapse_above_the_threshold_unless_control_forbids_it pins the divergent half rather than upstream's, and #438's commit body states the inverted rule as fact ("?v=false forces /32-per-peer even above the threshold"), so the error is in the decision logic and in its test and in its description, not in the mechanics. Everything else about #438 is right and should not be touched: 10000 as the constant, a strict > comparison, single-IP-in-CGNAT as the collapsible class matching Go's classify, the /10 replacing the /32s it covers, and the self and MagicDNS 100.100.100.100/32 routes kept distinct from the fold. The fix is one expression -- Some(false) must yield CGNAT_THRESHOLD, not usize::MAX -- plus re-pinning the merged test to upstream's rule, plus correcting the claim in the doc comment that records it. Assert the case that currently passes wrongly: with one-cgnat?v=false set AND more than 10000 distinct CGNAT peer routes, the route set must collapse to the single /10. This is host-OS-facing: no peer and no control plane observes the route table directly, which is why it is narrow rather than urgent -- but it is the unbounded route table #438 existed to bound, still reachable on control's say-so. Read it beside the sibling bead about the no-attribute platform gate: the two are halves of the same tri-state and are cheapest to port together, though neither blocks the other. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Apply upstream's platform and CGNAT-interface gate when no one-cgnat attribute is set
beads.description: With neither one-cgnat attribute present this node keeps one /32 per peer, where a Go client on the same OS installs a single /10. At commit e2ed432399c9b0fda7aa14e9eb27784d2d893c55, upstream does NOT fall through to the 10000 threshold when the attribute is absent. ipn/ipnlocal/local.go:6207 shouldUseOneCGNATRoute decides in order: consult the control knob first (an explicit true or false is TERMINAL and nothing below runs); then return true for versionOS == "plan9"; then for versionOS == "macOS" or "android" probe netmon.HasCGNATInterface() and return true when no OTHER interface uses the CGNAT range -- returning FALSE if that probe errors; and only otherwise false. A true result becomes routemanager.TailnetConfig.OneCGNAT (reached via local.go:6131), i.e. a threshold of 1, so the /10 replaces the per-peer /32s from the second CGNAT route onward. This repository has no platform or interface input anywhere on that path. The merged Node::one_cgnat() returns None whenever the attribute is absent, and cgnat_threshold(None) is unconditionally CGNAT_THRESHOLD; #438's commit body does not mention the gate. On macOS -- a platform this workspace builds and tests on -- this tree therefore keeps one /32 per peer at every peer count below 10000 where a Go client installs the single /10 and stops reconfiguring the host route set per peer. Two things to carry exactly, because they are the parts a port gets wrong. First, the ORDER: an explicit attribute is terminal, so the platform gate must run only when the attribute is absent -- if it runs first, one-cgnat?v=false stops working. Second, the ERROR DIRECTION: a failed HasCGNATInterface probe means FALSE (keep per-peer routes), not true; defaulting the other way would collapse the route set on a box whose interface state could not be read, which is the opposite of what upstream chose. Scope: plan9 is not a platform this workspace targets and can be recorded in a comment rather than implemented. The macOS arm is the one that matters here and is testable on this box; the android arm shares its code path and costs nothing extra once the probe exists. The probe itself -- does any interface other than the Tailscale one carry a 100.64.0.0/10 address -- is new capability for ts_netmon or ts_host_net and is the bulk of the work; the decision logic on top of it is a dozen lines. Assert all three: attribute present wins over platform; absent on macOS with no other CGNAT interface collapses; absent on macOS with the probe failing does not collapse. Read it beside the sibling bead about one-cgnat?v=false. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Divert every delta mechanism on disable-delta-updates, not only PeersChangedPatch
beads.description: Control's escape hatch off the incremental netmap path was ported and still cannot take this node off the incremental netmap path. At commit e2ed432399c9b0fda7aa14e9eb27784d2d893c55, upstream's gate is the FIRST statement of tryHandleIncrementally (control/controlclient/map.go:277-278, an early return of false when ms.controlKnobs is non-nil and ms.controlKnobs.DisableDeltaUpdates.Load() is set), and a false return there is NOT scoped to patches: handleNonKeepAliveMapResponse falls through to ms.netmap() and netmapUpdater.UpdateFullNetmap(nm) for the ENTIRE response, whatever it carried. That is what the attribute's own documentation asks for -- treat all netmap changes as "full" ones as tailscaled did in 1.48.x and earlier. In this repository, #442 put the check in PeerTracker::apply_peer_patch_set, which the netmap handler reaches only from inside a guard on msg.peer_patches being non-empty. But this tree has TWO delta mechanisms, not one. PeerTracker::apply_peer_update -- which applies PeerUpdate::Delta, built in ts_control::tokio::map_stream from MapResponse.PeersChanged and PeersRemoved -- runs unconditionally just above it and is untouched by the attribute. So a response carrying only PeersChanged/PeersRemoved never takes the full arm even with the attribute set, and a response carrying both applies the delta incrementally BEFORE the patches are rebuilt as a full update. The escape hatch exists precisely for the case where control has decided this client's incremental path cannot be trusted -- because control is emitting bad deltas, or because this client is applying them wrongly -- and covering one of two mechanisms does not achieve that. The fix is to move the gate rather than to add a second copy of it: it belongs above both appliers, at the one point the map response is dispatched, so that the attribute selects the full path for the whole response the way Go's single early return does. A second check inside apply_peer_update would reproduce the bug's shape -- two places that can disagree -- and is what to avoid. Keep what #442 got right, because its central claim is exactly Go's structure and is easy to lose in a refactor: the attribute neither REJECTS the response nor DROPS the deltas, it declines the incremental path so the full path handles the same response. A response carrying only PeersChanged must therefore still be applied under the attribute, as a full update; a test asserting such a response is ignored would pin the wrong behaviour. The timing claim also holds and should stay tested: UpdateFromNodeAttributes runs before the tryHandleIncrementally call, so an attribute control grants takes effect on the response that granted it. Assert the case that currently fails: a response carrying ONLY PeersChanged/PeersRemoved, with the attribute set, must take the full-rebuild arm. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Re-run the tailnet-lock filter on the full-netmap arm disable-delta-updates selects
beads.description: Declining the delta path is supposed to re-verify every peer against the tailnet lock, and here it verifies almost none. At commit e2ed432399c9b0fda7aa14e9eb27784d2d893c55, upstream reaches the full netmap path through b.tkaFilterNetmapLocked(st.NetMap) (ipn/ipnlocal/local.go:2011), guarded only by envknob.TKASkipSignatureCheck, immediately before setNetMapLocked. So taking the full arm re-verifies EVERY peer's node-key signature against the lock and evicts the ones that no longer verify. The delta path gets the narrower tkaFilterDeltaMutsLocked instead, and upstream's own comment says that exists precisely to match "the full-netmap behavior of tkaFilterNetmapLocked" -- i.e. the two arms are meant to reach the same trust verdict by different routes. In this repository, #442's rebuild_netmap_with_patches re-installs every retained peer through upsert_from_control without re-running the lock gate, so the only trust check on that arm is the per-patched-node one inside apply_peer_patches. A peer that was admitted earlier and whose signature has since stopped verifying is evicted by upstream on this path and retained here. This is filed as the smaller of the two #442 gaps and it is deliberately not filed as a security regression, because #442's DECISIONS section DISCLOSED the omission and gave a defensible reason: this tree rewrites an expiry-flagged peer's node key via ts_keys::node_public_with_bad_old_prefix, so a whole-database re-filter would evict that peer and lose the expiry diagnostic. That reason is real and the fix must not break it. It argues for a NARROWER gate rather than for no gate: re-run the lock filter over the retained set, exempting peers whose node key carries the bad-old-prefix rewrite, so an expiry-flagged peer keeps its diagnostic while a peer whose signature genuinely stopped verifying is evicted. Whoever takes this should confirm that exemption is expressible before writing it -- if it turns out the rewrite is not distinguishable at the point the filter runs, the honest outcome is to record THAT in PORTING.md as a deliberate divergence with its reason, which is a legitimate close for this bead rather than a failure. Assert both directions, because either alone is the bug: a peer whose node-key signature no longer verifies is dropped when the full arm runs, AND an expiry-flagged peer whose key was rewritten survives it with its diagnostic intact. Read it beside the sibling bead about which mechanisms the attribute diverts -- that one decides how often this arm runs at all, so landing it first makes this one testable. See PORTING.md section B.
